  g(x + a) = g(x) + b  for all x ∈ ℤ.

sentence: A “Modulo” Counting Argument
sentence-category-reason: Descriptive header naming the upcoming type of argument.

sentence: We will now use (★) to deduce a necessary relation between a and b.
sentence-category-reason: Announces the plan to use the derived relation (★) to find a condition on a and b.

sentence: Fix any integer x.
sentence-category-reason: Sets up the argument by fixing an arbitrary integer x.

sentence:
Then (★) tells us that
  f(x + b) = f(x) + a.
sentence-category-reason: Recalls the previously derived relation (★) for use in the argument.

sentence:
In particular, if you look at the value of f modulo a, you find that for any integer x,
  f(x + b) ≡ f(x)  (mod a).
sentence-category-reason: Infers a congruence modulo a from the relation in (★).

sentence: This means that f is “periodic modulo a” with period b; that is, if you know the value of f on a complete set of residues modulo b, then the value of f on any integer is determined modulo a.
sentence-category-reason: Explains the implication as periodicity modulo a and its consequence.

sentence: Since f is a bijection ℤ → ℤ, its image is all of ℤ.
sentence-category-reason: Uses the bijectivity of f to deduce its image is all integers.

sentence: In particular, every residue class modulo a must be hit by some value f(x).
sentence-category-reason: Draws a consequence about covering all residue classes modulo a.

sentence: However, if you know f only on b different starting values (one for each residue class modulo b), then the set of possible residues f(x) (mod a) can have at most b different values.
sentence-category-reason: Argues about the maximum number of residue classes modulo a achievable from b starting values.

sentence:
Therefore, we must have
  a ≤ b.
sentence-category-reason: Draws a logical inequality conclusion from prior argument.

sentence: Now, use the analogous relation for g.
sentence-category-reason: Announces the next step to apply the analogous argument to g.

sentence:
From
  g(x + a) = g(x) + b,
we deduce that g is “periodic modulo b” with period a.
sentence-category-reason: Deduces a property of g from the given relation.

sentence: Since g is bijective, its image is all of ℤ and in particular every residue class modulo b is attained.
sentence-category-reason: Uses established bijectivity of g to infer coverage of residue classes.

sentence: But g is determined by its values on a complete set of residues modulo a (of which there are a values), so there can be at most a different residues modulo b.
sentence-category-reason: Reasoning about residue classes to bound the number of residues attained.

sentence:
Hence,
  b ≤ a.
sentence-category-reason: Concludes the inequality from the preceding analysis.
Structural label marking a referenced result; not substantive reasoning.

Combining (1) and (2) we conclude that
  a = b.
sentence-category-reason: Combines two inequalities to conclude equality.

sentence: Sufficiency
sentence-category-reason: Section heading indicating the goal to prove sufficiency.

sentence: It remains to show that if a = b then there do indeed exist functions f and g satisfying (1) and (2).
sentence-category-reason: States the plan to prove existence given a = b.

sentence:
For example, if we set
  f(x) = x + c  and  g(x) = x + (a – c)
for any integer c, then
  f(g(x)) = (x + (a – c)) + c = x + a,
and
  g(f(x)) = (x + c) + (a – c) = x + a.
sentence-category-reason: Constructs explicit functions and verifies the equations via calculations.

sentence: Thus, when a = b the equations are satisfied.
sentence-category-reason: Confirms that the constructed functions satisfy the required equations.

sentence: There are, of course, many other (even non‐linear) solutions, but the existence of at least one solution shows that the condition a = b is also sufficient.
sentence-category-reason: Explains why existence of one example establishes sufficiency; conceptual reasoning.
Section heading marking the concluding part.

sentence: The functions f and g exist if and only if a = b.
sentence-category-reason: States the final iff condition answering the problem.

sentence:
Equivalently, the only pairs (a, b) ∈ ℤ × ℤ for which there exist functions f, g : ℤ → ℤ satisfying
  f(g(x)) = x + a  and  g(f(x)) = x + b  for all x ∈ ℤ
are those of the form
  (a, b) = (c, c)  for some integer c.
sentence-category-reason: Restates the final answer in equivalent form.
Section heading introducing the final answer.

sentence: All pairs (a, b) that work are exactly those with a = b; that is, (a, b) = (c, c) for some c ∈ ℤ.
sentence-category-reason: Gives the final answer succinctly.
